job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Adam Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at 7, toast, then the 8:10 train to Wexley from the house in Carrow where I rent a room with three others. I work at Girard & Sons, a small accountancy with six staff. I'm a trainee bookkeeper, so I enter receipts, reconcile bank accounts and file returns for corner shops and plumbers. It's steady work and I like knowing exactly what's expected. I finish at 5:30, cook, watch football and don't think about my loan, which is 34,000.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, that's what I thought. At work I'd tell Mr. Girard, who owns the firm, that we carry on as we are. With friends I'd just shrug, because I don't have strong views on the hype either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel a bit relieved but my money is tight. I earn 23,000 and my room costs 430, so after the loan and food there's not much left. The firm is also quite old. Mr. Girard is 61, and if he retires and sells up, nobody knows what happens to the juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. I'd finish my bookkeeping certificate, which the firm pays for, and put 30 a month aside. I'd ask Mr. Girard in a year what the plans are for the firm. I wouldn't go looking elsewhere unless I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, basically. Not happy, not worried. It's the feeling of a long, grey week at the office, which I don't mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody knows what happens if Mr. Girard sells. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. It's the one thing I can't control. If a bigger firm took over, they'd probably bring in their own people and their own systems, and I'd be the new one with the least experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay as long as they'd have me and look quietly for another bookkeeping place in Wexley or Harbury. There are only about three suitable firms around here, so I couldn't be fussy.

say: I'd tell Mr. Girard (the firm's owner) we carry on as we are.
think: I'm relieved but money is **tight**: 23,000 pay against 430 rent and a 34,000 loan.
The firm is old and if Mr. Girard **sells up** nobody knows what happens to juniors.
do: Finish the bookkeeping **certificate** the firm pays for.
Put **30 a month** aside and ask Mr. Girard about the firm's plans in a year.
feel: **Okay**, like a long grey week at the office, which I don't mind.

fieldNote: The risk he names is **ownership** of the firm, not technology.
Likes **routine** and spells out what's expected, in line with his resistance to change.

steps.text: Keep reconciling bank accounts and filing returns at Girard & Sons
Finish the bookkeeping certificate the firm is paying for
Put 30 a month aside from pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll believe it when I see it in our office. If the others at work talked about it, I'd say it'll take years to get to a place like Girard & Sons. I don't use the tools and I don't plan to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's coming for my kind of work. Entering receipts and reconciling accounts is exactly what the card lists, checking and planning. I'm worried the firm will quietly stop training new people. And I'm not the one who'd pick up the new software first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what the firm tells me to do, and no more. If Mr. Girard buys a program, I'd learn it from the manual, slowly, and ask Faye, the senior, to show me. I'd keep saving and avoid new debts. I wouldn't change jobs on a guess, because a job is a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, like standing on ice that might be thick or thin. I don't like not knowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Faye uses the tools already. Why not learn from her now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. I suppose I don't like feeling like the slow one next to her. And I don't trust the answers it gives. I'd probably start with one small thing, like the receipts scanner, if Mr. Girard asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the firm said they were cutting one trainee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd assume it was me, since I'm the newest. I'd ask for a reference straight away and start applying across the county. And I'd tell my parents, who'd tell me to come home, which I wouldn't want.

S1.quote: I'd assume it was me, since I'm the newest.
fieldNote: **Public** scepticism and private worry differ clearly.

steps.text: Ask Faye to show me the receipt scanner at work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? I'd say that's hard to believe, but if it's true then nobody's ready. I'd say the people in charge should say so plainly. I'd keep my head down at work and not make noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think that's the end of what I trained for. Bookkeeping's the kind of thing a machine does in seconds. I've 34,000 of debt, under a month of pay saved, and I'm not the kind to jump into a new field. I'd feel stuck, and I'd feel stupid for picking a degree that aged so fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything I can: no football league, no takeaways, a cheaper room if I can find one. I'd try for any job that isn't on a screen, maybe in a warehouse or the delivery depot in Harbury, where robots come later. And I'd ask the council what support exists. I wouldn't do anything dramatic, because I don't know what dramatic would even be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frozen, honestly. It's like waiting for a letter you know is bad news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel stupid for picking the degree. Who else would think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, probably, though he'd never say it. He drives a bus and he told me once that a trade is safer than a degree. I didn't listen. I'd have to face that conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first month look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd phone my loan company, check my rent notice, and take any extra shift going at the depot. I'd tell the lads in the house I might have to move out. And I'd probably still go to the office every day, in case it all turns out slower than they say.

say: If it's true, then nobody is **ready**, and the people in charge should say so.
I'd keep my head down at work and not make **noise**.

feel: **Frozen**, like waiting for a letter you know is bad news.

fieldNote: Freezes rather than **acts**; his plan is cuts and any available work.

steps.text: Drop the football league and takeaways and find a cheaper room
Take extra shifts at the Harbury delivery depot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to prepare if people actually do. I'd say employers should say what they'll do, and I'd keep my own opinion mostly to myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's a bit like the two-year one but with more room to breathe. I'd probably still be at Girard & Sons for a couple of years, which helps me clear a bit of the loan. Then I'd have to leave bookkeeping anyway, I'd guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do two things. First I'd save hard, 100 a month, and avoid any new spending. Second I'd quietly sign up for an evening course in something practical, like logistics or surveying, maybe at the college in Harbury. I'd keep the day job meanwhile. I'd start in about a year, not now, because I'd want to see if the news changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but manageable. A bit like exam time. Not pleasant, but at least I know how long it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait a year before starting a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm cautious. I've seen people jump at things that turned out to be nothing. If the news in a year still says it's on track, I'd move. I know that's slow, and slow might cost me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mr. Girard told us he was selling, or if Faye's workload started dropping because of software. Something I can see in the office, not something on the news.

say: Five years is long enough to **prepare** if people do.
Employers should say what they'll do, and I'd keep my own **opinion** to myself.
think: It's like the two-year picture with more room to **breathe**.
I'd probably still have to **leave** bookkeeping in the end.
do: Save **100 a month** and avoid new spending.
Sign up for an evening **logistics** or surveying course at the Harbury college in about a year.
feel: **Anxious** but manageable, like exam time where at least I know how long it is.
S3.quote: I've seen people jump at things that turned out to be nothing.
fieldNote: **Cautious** by habit: he wants proof in the office before moving.
Chooses practical, **hands-on** fields, a sensible hedge on the robot timeline.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening logistics course at Harbury college in a year
Stay in the Girard & Sons job while studying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd say, that's long, so people shouldn't panic. I'd say the government has time to set things up and workers have time to adjust, if they want to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel better. By 2036 I'd be 32, I could be out of debt and into something else. I'd still be more nervous than most, because I don't change easily. But time is something I'm good with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and clear the loan first, aiming for about three years. Then I'd start a course in something I'm drawn to, maybe property management or surveying. I'd try the AI tools around year three, once the rest of the office is using them. And I'd save for a deposit, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not too bad. A bit uneasy, but it feels like a normal life with a big thing in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try the tools around year three. Why then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because by then the bugs are out and everyone knows what's useful. I don't want to be first, I'd rather be steady. I think that's the right way for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would that be too late, for a job in finance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Possibly, yes. That's the risk of my way. But I'd have the course and my clear debt as a backup. That's more than I'd have in the two-year world.

The government has time to set things up and workers have time to **adjust**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I don't change fast, and two years gives me no room to be slow. What would help is a short, clear warning from the government and a course I can take that's paid for, not something I have to take on more debt for.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really. Just that people like me aren't against change. We just need to see it working before we jump, and we need to have enough money to be patient.

headlineQuote: We just need to see it working before we jump, and we need to have enough money to be patient.
portrait: **Adam** is 22, an accounting graduate working as a trainee bookkeeper at a six-person firm in Wexley.
He rents a room in Carrow, owes **34,000** and has under a month of pay saved.
He is centrist, prefers routine and has **never used AI**, waiting until he sees it working in the office.
He turns to **hands-on** or practical work in the fast scenarios and plans slowly in the slow ones.
Time helps him most: **alarmed** at two years, only uneasy at ten.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because he changes slowly and two years leaves no room to be slow.
whatWouldHelp: A short, clear **warning** from the government and a paid course so he needn't take on new debt.
Enough money to be **patient** until he sees the change working.
